title: Jake Holloway — Energy Supplier Switch Experience
summary: Jake, a 22-year-old junior developer in a shared house, takes on the responsibility of switching his household's energy provider. He navigates comparing tariffs online, coordinating agreement with three housemates via WhatsApp, completing a fully digital registration, and establishing bill-splitting via Monzo. His journey is shaped by his preference for efficient digital processes colliding with the messy reality of group decision-making and an industry that still expects phone-based interactions. Despite the coordination friction, Jake successfully completes the switch and establishes an ongoing routine, proving to himself he can handle adult responsibilities.

lanes.label: Need at Step
lanes.description: What Jake specifically needs at this moment — the micro-emergence of his traits meeting the service touchpoint

lanes.label: Pain at Step
lanes.description: How this step causes pain for Jake — the gap between his need and what the service provides

lanes.label: Opportunities
lanes.description: Improvement opportunities specific to Jake's experience

actions: Receives email from current provider about rate increase
Checks Reddit and MoneySavingExpert to understand if this is normal
laneContent.thoughts: This seems like a lot more than my mates are paying. I should probably look into switching - isn't that what adults do?
laneContent.needAtStep: Quick confirmation that switching is the right move and that the rate increase is genuinely above market — validation that his instinct to act is correct
laneContent.painAtStep: Jake's first encounter with 'adulting' territory he was never taught about. The rate increase letter uses jargon he's not fully confident with, triggering his frustration with unnecessarily complicated processes.

actions: Googles 'how to switch energy provider UK'
Reads MoneySavingExpert guides
Checks if landlord permission is needed for rental property
laneContent.thoughts: This seems more complicated than I expected. Do I need to tell the landlord? What about the meter readings? At least I can do this all online.

barriers.description: Uncertainty about rental property rules for switching — unclear if landlord approval is needed
barriers.workarounds: Researches online, finds that tenants can usually switch without landlord permission if paying bills directly
barriers.emergesFrom: Jake's first-time experience with utility management combined with the shared tenancy complexity creates knowledge gaps about permissions and responsibilities

laneContent.needAtStep: A clear, jargon-free answer to 'can I actually do this as a renter in a shared house?' — he needs permission and process clarity before he can commit his research energy
laneContent.painAtStep: The information he finds is scattered across multiple sources and written for a general audience, not specifically for young renters in shared houses. His analytical style wants a clear decision tree but the guidance is ambiguous.

actions: Uses comparison websites to find deals
Filters for no exit fees for tenancy flexibility
Screenshots best options to share with housemates
laneContent.thoughts: PowerGrid Energy looks good - decent app reviews, no exit fees, and the price is competitive. Their app looks modern too. I'll put together a comparison for the house WhatsApp.

barriers.description: Confusing tariff structures make like-for-like comparison difficult
barriers.workarounds: Uses MSE's comparison tool which standardises calculations
barriers.emergesFrom: Jake's analytical decision-making style clashes with the industry's complex pricing — he wants clear data but tariffs obscure true costs

laneContent.needAtStep: A way to quickly generate a clear, shareable comparison that his housemates (who care less about details) can understand and approve in minutes, not days
opportunities: Create shareable comparison cards optimised for messaging apps
Highlight key differentiators relevant to renters (exit fees, app quality, bill-splitting)

momentThatMatters.description: Finding a deal that balances cost savings with no exit fees — important for rental flexibility

actions: Posts comparison in house WhatsApp
Chases responses over several days
Eventually calls a quick house meeting to finalise decision
laneContent.thoughts: Why is it so hard to get everyone to respond? Tom's read the messages but not replied. I just want to get this sorted so we can stop overpaying.

barriers.description: Coordinating decisions with 4 people with different priorities and availability is time-consuming and frustrating
barriers.workarounds: Sets a deadline and arranges brief in-person chat to force decision
barriers.emergesFrom: Jake's desire for efficient, path-of-least-resistance processes directly conflicts with the multi-stakeholder coordination required by the shared house context

laneContent.needAtStep: A mechanism to get a quick 'yes' from everyone without it turning into an endless group chat debate — he needs to convert his research into a decision without losing momentum
laneContent.painAtStep: Jake has done the hard work of researching and comparing, but now he's stuck waiting for three other people who don't share his urgency. His research-then-act pattern breaks down when the 'act' requires group consensus. Every day of delay feels like money wasted on the old tariff.

momentThatMatters.description: The point where research meets group decision-making — success here unlocks progress

laneContent.thoughts: Finally, everyone's agreed. PowerGrid it is. Let me get this done before anyone changes their mind.

actions: Navigates to PowerGrid Energy website from comparison site link
Clicks 'Switch to us' and enters postcode
laneContent.thoughts: Good, I can do this all online. The website looks decent - not some janky old thing. Let's see how easy this actually is.

actions: Enters name, email, phone number reluctantly
Provides property details including current meter readings
Selects tariff and payment method
laneContent.thoughts: Wait, I have to give a phone number? I hope they don't call me. And being the 'account holder' means I'm responsible for the whole bill... what if someone doesn't pay their share?

barriers.description: Phone number is a required field even though Jake prefers digital-only contact
barriers.workarounds: Enters number but immediately sets communication preferences to email/app only in settings
barriers.emergesFrom: Jake's strong aversion to phone calls meets the provider's data collection requirements

barriers.description: Uncertainty about personal liability as account holder if housemates don't pay their share
barriers.workarounds: Plans to set up a shared pot or payment app to collect money upfront each month
barriers.emergesFrom: Jake's need to avoid unexpected costs and be seen as reliable intensifies the liability concern inherent in the shared-house account holder role

laneContent.needAtStep: Reassurance that being the named account holder won't leave him financially exposed — he needs to understand the risk before he commits
laneContent.painAtStep: The form forces him to confront the financial risk of being the sole liable party. The provider gives no guidance on shared household arrangements, treating this like a single-person account setup. His security need is directly threatened.

momentThatMatters.description: Realising he'll be personally liable for the whole bill as the named account holder

actions: Completes online identity check
Enters details from driving licence
Answers security questions
laneContent.thoughts: Okay, standard KYC stuff. At least I don't have to post documents or anything. Pretty smooth so far.

actions: Submits application
Sees message that credit check is being performed
laneContent.thoughts: Credit check? I've only had a credit card for a year. What if I fail? That would be embarrassing to tell the others.

barriers.description: Uncertainty about credit check criteria for first-time account holders with limited credit history
barriers.workarounds: None available — just has to wait and hope
barriers.emergesFrom: Jake's need for control and to avoid surprises clashes with the opaque credit assessment process — his thin credit file as a recent graduate adds genuine uncertainty

laneContent.needAtStep: Transparency about what the credit check involves and whether his thin credit history is likely to be a problem — he needs to manage the risk of embarrassment before it materialises
laneContent.painAtStep: The credit check is a black box. Jake has no way to predict the outcome, and failure would mean going back to his housemates empty-handed after promising he'd handle it. His need for recognition as capable is directly at stake.

momentThatMatters.description: Waiting for credit check result — anxiety about whether first-time applicant will be approved

actions: Receives on-screen confirmation that credit check passed
Proceeds to payment setup
laneContent.thoughts: Yes! Passed. Okay, I can actually do this adult stuff. Now let's get the payment sorted.

momentThatMatters.description: Credit check passed — validation that he can handle adult financial responsibilities

actions: Enters bank details for Direct Debit
Sets up Monzo shared pot with housemates
Sends invites to all housemates with monthly contribution amount
laneContent.thoughts: Direct Debit from my account, then collect from everyone via Monzo. This should work - we already split Netflix this way. Setting reminder to chase if anyone misses payment.
laneContent.needAtStep: A bill-splitting mechanism that automates collection so he doesn't become the household nag — he needs the social dynamic to stay comfortable
opportunities: Offer in-app bill-splitting that sends payment requests directly to housemates
Integrate with popular fintech apps for automated collection

momentThatMatters.description: Setting up bill-splitting arrangement with housemates — sets the tone for ongoing payment dynamics

actions: Downloads PowerGrid app
Sets notification preferences to email and app push only
Enables paperless billing
laneContent.thoughts: Finally, an energy company with a decent app. Push notifications for bills, email for important stuff, definitely no phone calls. Perfect.

actions: Receives welcome email with account details and switch timeline
Checks app to see account status
Forwards key dates to house WhatsApp
laneContent.thoughts: Nice, clear timeline of what happens next. Switch completes in about 3 weeks. Just need to submit final meter reading on switch day.

actions: Waits during 14-day cooling off period
Checks app occasionally to see progress
Receives notification that cooling off has ended
laneContent.thoughts: Good to know I could have cancelled if needed. Now it's definitely happening. Just need to remember the meter reading on switch day.

actions: Receives app notification that today is switch day
Takes photos of meter readings
Submits via app
Asks Tom to let him into room with second meter
laneContent.thoughts: Okay, meter reading time. App makes this easy - just take a photo. Done. Now we're officially with PowerGrid.

actions: Receives first bill notification via app
Reviews charges and confirms tariff matches
Screenshots and sends to house WhatsApp with 'your share' amounts
Checks Monzo pot has funds
laneContent.thoughts: First bill looks right - the tariff rate matches what we signed up for. Breaking it into quarters for everyone. We're actually saving money compared to before!
laneContent.needAtStep: Confirmation that the deal is as promised and that he can demonstrate the savings to his housemates — proof that his effort was worth it
opportunities: Show savings comparison vs previous provider directly in the app
Generate shareable bill breakdown for household groups

momentThatMatters.description: Receiving first bill confirmation that the switch worked and pricing is as expected — validation of the entire effort

actions: Sets up monthly reminder to check Monzo pot before Direct Debit
Enables usage alerts in app
Bookmarks how to submit meter readings
laneContent.thoughts: Okay, this is manageable. Monthly check that everyone's paid, keep an eye on usage. I've actually got this adulting thing sorted.

barriers.description: Ongoing administrative burden of collecting money from housemates each month
barriers.workarounds: Automated Monzo scheduled payments from each housemate reduce chase effort
barriers.emergesFrom: Jake's desire for efficient, low-friction processes will be tested monthly by the account holder collection responsibility — mitigated by smart use of fintech tools

laneContent.needAtStep: An autopilot system that handles the recurring admin so he can maintain the household harmony without becoming the money-chaser
laneContent.painAtStep: Even with Monzo automating most of it, Jake knows he'll need to monitor and chase if anyone's payment bounces. The ongoing vigilance is a low-grade tax on the social dynamic he values.

outcome.reflection: Jake successfully navigated his first energy switch, proving to himself and his housemates that he can handle adult responsibilities. The hardest part wasn't the provider process itself — which was largely smooth and digital — but the coordination overhead of getting housemates aligned and establishing fair payment routines. The experience would have been significantly improved by built-in bill-splitting and clearer guidance for shared households.
